lede: Formula 1 rewrote its rulebook for 2026, with engines that take half their power from the battery, wings that open on the straights and smaller, lighter cars, and Mercedes read it best. Kimi Antonelli, 20, has won nine of the 18 races and leaves Austin with 365 points, 123 clear of his teammate George Russell with five rounds and 125 points left; he can be champion in Mexico City on November 1. Behind them, Lewis Hamilton has his first win in a Ferrari, Max Verstappen won back to back in Malaysia and Singapore, and the reigning champion Lando Norris has two. The newcomers, Audi (which took over Sauber) and Cadillac, have found it hard going, and war in the Middle East wiped out April's races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia; Bahrain's was run in Malaysia instead.

rounds.headline: Russell opens the new era with a Mercedes one-two
rounds.report: Russell made a poor launch and swapped the lead with Leclerc several times in the opening laps. A virtual safety car on lap 12 for Hadjar's stopped Red Bull let Mercedes switch both cars to hards while the Ferraris stayed out, and Russell then made a one-stop race work and pulled clear to win by about three seconds in a Mercedes one-two. Battery management on Melbourne's long straights dominated the first race of the new rules, and five cars failed to finish. [1][2][3]

rounds.headline: Antonelli, 19, wins his first grand prix
rounds.report: Hamilton jumped from third into the lead at the start, but Antonelli was back in front before the end of lap 2. A safety car for Stroll's stopped Aston Martin let Antonelli make his only stop for hards without losing the lead, while Russell struggled for tyre temperature at the restart and fell behind the Ferraris for a time. Antonelli survived a late lock-up to win by 5.5 seconds for his first Grand Prix victory. [1][2]

Oliver Bearman's heavy crash at Spoon on lap 22, after he took to the grass to avoid a much slower Alpine, brought out the safety car just as Antonelli was due to stop. He pitted under it, led from the lap 28 restart and pulled away to make it two wins in a row. [1][2]

rounds.report: The start was moved three hours earlier to beat forecast storms that never arrived. Antonelli locked up into Turn 1 and handed Leclerc the lead, retook it on lap 4, and then held off Norris, who could not get close enough in the turbulent air to attack. Two early safety cars, for Gasly's roll after contact with Lawson and Hadjar's crash, bunched the field, and Leclerc spun out of third on the final lap. [1][2]

rounds.report: Antonelli ran a long first stint and built a lead of almost 30 seconds. storylines.title: Antonelli on the brink of a record title
storylines.body: Kimi Antonelli won his first Grand Prix in China as a teenager, took the championship lead in Japan as the youngest leader in F1 history, and has nine wins and seven poles from 18 rounds. Even a mid-season wobble (a retirement in Barcelona and a 15th at Silverstone) never cost him the lead, and wins from 19th at Monza and in Madrid put him out of reach of most rivals. He leaves Austin 123 points clear of Russell and can clinch in Mexico City. He would be F1's youngest champion and Italy's first since 1953. [1][2][3][4]

storylines.title: Mercedes mastered the 2026 reset
storylines.body: The all-new rules (no MGU-H, a near 50-50 split between combustion and electric power, sustainable fuel, smaller cars and active aero in place of DRS) produced a clear early pecking order with Mercedes on top. The works team won the first six races and 12 of 18 overall, and leads Ferrari by 133 points in the constructors' table. Mercedes-powered McLaren is the only other team to win with that engine, while Red Bull's in-house Ford-backed unit took until October to win. Ferrari and its customers have won only twice. [1][2][3]

storylines.title: Energy management row and the FIA's in-season fixes
storylines.body: From Melbourne onward, drivers had to lift and coast to recharge batteries that supply about half the car's power, and some circuits exposed that badly. At Suzuka, Bearman suffered a 50G crash after running into a large speed difference with a car that was harvesting energy, and drivers including Alonso criticised the rules openly. The FIA met the power unit makers four times in April and, before Miami, raised the 'super clipping' limit to 350kW and cut the qualifying harvest allowance from 8MJ to 7MJ. Battery deployment still decided battles as late as Monza. [1][2][3][4]

storylines.title: War redraws the calendar
storylines.body: Escalating conflict involving Iran forced the cancellation of April's Bahrain and Saudi Arabian rounds, announced around the Chinese GP, and the calendar briefly fell to 22 races. In late July, F1 and the FIA agreed to run the Bahrain GP at Sepang in Malaysia on 4 October, keeping Bahrain as promoter and bringing the season back to 23 rounds. Saudi Arabia was never reinstated. The Qatar and Abu Dhabi finale stayed in doubt for months, with Imola as a fallback, until Domenicali confirmed both in early October subject to security assurances. A mid-October deadline then passed with no change. [1][2][3][4]

storylines.title: Hamilton's breakthrough and Ferrari's near-misses
storylines.body: Hamilton took his first Grand Prix podium for Ferrari in China and his first win for the team in Barcelona, where an aggressive three-stop strategy and a well-timed virtual safety car beat Mercedes. Leclerc added victory at Silverstone, and Ferrari is a solid second in the constructors' table. Costly errors have held them back, though: Hamilton's ignored pit call in Singapore cost a podium, and pit-lane and collision penalties hurt him in Hungary and Belgium. He is still one of only two drivers who can mathematically catch Antonelli. [1][2][3]

storylines.title: Verstappen and Red Bull-Ford's autumn revival
storylines.body: Red Bull's first season with its own Ford-backed power unit started roughly: Verstappen crashed in Melbourne qualifying, retired in China, stalled and retired in Monaco, and crashed out at both Silverstone and Zandvoort. Steady podiums from Austria onward came before a breakthrough in October, with wins in the rain at Sepang and a clean sweep in Singapore on his 250th start. Hadjar has backed him up with podiums in Monaco and Baku, and Red Bull edges McLaren for third in the constructors' table on countback. [1][2][3][4]

storylines.title: The Monaco pit-lane timing saga
storylines.body: Gasly finished third in Monaco on the road but was dropped to seventh for two pit-lane speeding offences. Alpine won a right of review in June after a 77cm discrepancy was found in the pit-lane timing loops, and his podium was restored. McLaren and Red Bull, whose drivers had served similar penalties during the race, took the case to the FIA International Court of Appeal. After an August hearing, the court reinstated the penalties because Alpine could not prove Gasly's path was longer than measured. Hadjar keeps the podium. [1][2]

storylines.title: Hard landings for Cadillac, Audi and Aston Martin-Honda
storylines.body: New entrant Cadillac, running Ferrari engines with veterans Perez and Bottas, is the only team without a point after 18 rounds, and both cars have been regular retirements. Audi's first season as a works team has brought 23 points and eighth place. Aston Martin's new partnership with Honda has delivered just seven points, and Stroll's car has stopped on track often enough to trigger neutralisations in China, Monza, Madrid and Singapore. Midfield reports still describe the car as short on power. [1][2][3][4]

storylines.title: Red Bull family reshuffle and a rookie at Racing Bulls
storylines.body: Hadjar moved up to Red Bull alongside Verstappen for 2026, Tsunoda became reserve, and F2 graduate Arvid Lindblad took the Racing Bulls seat. Lawson's strong form has made him ninth in the standings, ahead of every driver outside the top four teams. [1][2][3]

storylines.body: The Spanish GP moved to the new Madring circuit around Madrid's IFEMA exhibition centre on a 10-year deal, while Barcelona kept a separate Barcelona-Catalunya GP. title.text: Five rounds remain (Mexico City, Sao Paulo, Las Vegas, Qatar, Abu Dhabi), none of them sprints, so each driver can score at most 125 more points (25 for a race win; no fastest-lap point in 2026; sprint wins, worth 8, are finished for the year). Antonelli has 365. Russell (242) can reach 367 at most and Hamilton (241) 366, so only those two can still beat him. Verstappen (max 361), Leclerc (358) and Norris (336) are eliminated. Ties are decided by most wins, and Antonelli's nine beats any total Russell (8 max) or Hamilton (6 max) could reach. So Russell must win all five races with Antonelli scoring no more than one point in total, and Hamilton must win all five with Antonelli scoring nothing. In Mexico, Antonelli is champion unless Russell wins with Antonelli 10th or lower, or Hamilton wins with Antonelli outside the points. Cancelling any remaining round would only make the leader's job easier. The arithmetic is The Watch’s, from the official standings and the published points system. [1][2][3]

calendar: The 2026 season was announced with 24 rounds. Bahrain and Saudi Arabia (originally April) were cancelled because of the Middle East conflict. On 26 July 2026 F1 brought the Bahrain Grand Prix back, staged at Sepang, Malaysia, on 2-4 October, which makes 23 rounds. Saudi Arabia was not replaced. As of late July and August 2026, F1 said Qatar and Abu Dhabi were confirmed and sold out, with a European finale (Imola reported) kept as a contingency. The six Sprint weekends are China, Miami, Canada, Britain, Netherlands and Singapore. Rounds 1-18 have been run; the next race is Mexico City (30 Oct-1 Nov). [1][2][3][4][5][6]
